faqs.question: How many words is a 2 minute Ganesh Chaturthi speech?
faqs.answer: About 200 to 240 words. Speeches are delivered at roughly 100 to 120 words a minute, so two minutes is a 200-240 word budget. Anything near 360 words is a two-minute read but a three-minute speech.

faqs.question: How do I start a Ganesh Chaturthi speech?
faqs.answer: Greet the room, then say how many points you have. "Good morning, respected teachers and my dear friends — today I want to tell you three things about Ganesh Chaturthi" gives the hall a map in one sentence, which a listener needs and a reader does not.

faqs.question: Is a Ganesh Chaturthi speech the same as an essay?
faqs.answer: No. An essay is measured in words and can be re-read; a speech is measured in minutes and is heard once. The same text that fills a 200-word essay brief will not fill a two-minute slot, and a 500-word essay read aloud runs close to five minutes.

faqs.question: How fast should I speak in a school assembly?
faqs.answer: Around 100 to 120 words a minute, which is the rate interpreting research treats as optimal for English speeches. It feels slow when you are nervous, because nerves push the rate up.

faqs.question: Should I memorise the speech word for word?
faqs.answer: Better to memorise the structure and the opening and closing lines, and keep the middle slightly loose. Word-for-word memorisation makes a single stumble unrecoverable, while a remembered map lets you rebuild the sentence live.

faqs.question: What is the best way to practise a speech?
faqs.answer: Out loud, not silently. Reading aloud produces measurably better memory than reading silently, and this has been tested in 7- to 10-year-olds across two experiments with 41 and 40 children. Record one run and check the clock against your word budget.

faqs.question: How long should a Ganesh Chaturthi speech be for school?
faqs.answer: Two minutes is the usual assembly slot, which is 200 to 240 words. Three minutes gets you 300 to 360. Five minutes is longer than most morning assemblies allow, so confirm the slot before you write to it.

faqs.question: Can I use the same script in Hindi or Marathi?
faqs.answer: Not by translating it word for word. Languages trade syllable rate against how much each syllable carries, converging on a similar information rate, so the same two minutes holds a different number of words. Draft in the language you will speak, then time it aloud.

faqs.question: What should a 10 line Ganesh Chaturthi speech cover?
faqs.answer: Ten lines is roughly a one-minute slot, so about 100 to 120 words: a greeting, who Ganesha is, the ten days and Anant Chaturdashi, the visarjan, and a closing Ganpati Bappa Morya. Drop the birth story and the personal line at that length.

faqs.question: What do I cut first if my speech is too long?
faqs.answer: Cut the third point's supporting detail and any adjective doing no work, but never the numbered signposts or the closing line. Losing the map costs the hall more than losing a fact.

faqs.question: Is Ganesh Chaturthi 2026 on the 14th of September?
faqs.answer: Yes, Ganesh Chaturthi 2026 falls on Monday 14 September, and the ten days end at Anant Chaturdashi. If your speech names the date, name the day of the week too — it is the detail an assembly audience actually registers.

faqs.question: Should I write my own speech or read one out?
faqs.answer: Write your own last two sentences at minimum. The line about what happens in your own house on the tenth day is the only part nobody else in the assembly can give, and it is the part people remember.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganesh Chaturthi Speech: What Fits in Two Minutes Aloud

A two-minute Ganesh Chaturthi speech is **200 to 240 words** — not a page of essay. Speeches are delivered at roughly 100 to 120 words a minute, while a fluent reader reads the same text aloud at 183 wpm, so a script that looks like two minutes on paper overruns badly when it is spoken. Below is a 220-word script timed to that rate, a three-minute extension, and a rehearsal method with evidence behind it.

What we can and cannot add: SubhSandesh has 3,894 personalised pages created since 2026-03-12, across 15 page types, and 49.6% of shared pages are opened on a phone (22,817 of 46,005 views). But no Ganesh Chaturthi page-creation data exists at all — the template went live 2026-09-10, four days before the festival on Monday 14 September 2026. The timing here comes from published research, with the arithmetic shown.

## What a Ganesh Chaturthi speech is, and where the essay stops helping

A Ganesh Chaturthi speech is a spoken text of one to three minutes, delivered aloud to a school assembly, that says who Ganesha is, why the festival runs ten days, and what the visarjan means. It is not a shortened essay: it is measured in minutes, heard once, and usually delivered from memory by a child in front of people watching.

Those constraints change the writing. An essay can be re-read at whatever pace the reader likes; a speech is graded on whether the hall follows it the first time. An essay brief says "200 words"; a speech brief says "two minutes" — and until you convert that into words, you do not have a brief at all.

## The word budget: turning minutes into words

Interpreting research puts the optimal delivery rate for an English speech at [100 to 120 words per minute](https://www.jostrans.org/article/view/7402) — the figure simultaneous interpreters use to judge whether a speaker is too fast. Budget against it: that is the rate a room actually takes speech in.

Reading is much faster. Marc Brysbaert's meta-analysis of 77 studies and 5,965 participants puts the [average oral reading rate at 183 wpm](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0749596X19300786), against 238 wpm for silent non-fiction; rates are lower for children, though he publishes no per-age figure and neither will we.

That 183-against-110 gap is why school speeches overrun: time your draft off the page and you have timed it at reading speed.

| Slot the school gives you | Word budget at 100–120 wpm | The same text read aloud at 183 wpm | What that budget holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 minute | 100–120 words | 183 words | A greeting, one idea, a closing line |
| 2 minutes | 200–240 words | 366 words | Three short points, signposted |
| 3 minutes | 300–360 words | 549 words | Three points, a story, one personal line |

Column two is your ceiling; column three is the trap. A 366-word draft feels like two minutes at your desk and lands past three on stage.

## A two-minute Ganesh Chaturthi speech, timed at 220 words

At 220 words, mid-band for a two-minute slot. The count is announced up front and each point numbered aloud, because a listener cannot look back.

> Good morning, respected teachers and my dear friends.
>
> Today is Ganesh Chaturthi, and I want to tell you three things: who we are welcoming, why he stays ten days, and what we do on the last one.
>
> First, who. Ganesha is the one with the elephant's head, the one we call Vighnaharta — the remover of obstacles. Before a wedding, before an exam, before the first page of a new notebook, his name comes first. He is the god of beginnings.
>
> Second, why ten days. The festival starts on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada and ends on Anant Chaturdashi. For those ten days Ganesha is not a picture on a wall. He is a guest in the house. Somebody wakes him, offers him modak, sings his aarti in the evening, and says goodnight. In some houses that job usually belongs to the youngest person who can be trusted with a diya.
>
> Third, the last day. We carry him to the water and let him go, and we say: Ganpati Bappa Morya, pudhchya varshi lavkar ya. Come back soon next year. We practise letting go of the murti so that letting go of other things gets easier.
>
> So when you fold your hands today, ask him for one obstacle removed. Just one.
>
> Ganpati Bappa Morya. Thank you.

## The three-minute version: additions, not a rewrite

To reach 300 to 360 words, do not rewrite. Add three blocks of about 40 words and leave every signpost where it is: the birth story in four sentences between points one and two, one line on the clay murti and the visarjan after point three, and a single personal sentence about what happens in your own house on the tenth day.

That last one is the sentence people remember, and the only one nobody else in the assembly can give. Keep it concrete: a name, a dish, a room.

## What a listener needs that a reader does not

A reader who loses the thread scrolls back. A listener cannot, so the speech must carry its own map — the work "I want to tell you three things" does: it tells the hall how many landings there are.

There is a ceiling on what you can push through, too. Brysbaert concludes reading rates line up with maximum listening speed, and Coupé and colleagues found that across [17 languages information rate converges on about 39 bits per second](https://advances.sciencemag.org/content/advances/5/9/eaaw2594.full.pdf) despite very different syllable rates. Speaking faster does not deliver more; the surplus is lost.

So: number your points aloud, repeat the closing phrase, and put the line that matters at the very end.

## Giving it in Hindi or Marathi changes the words, not the minutes

The two minutes stay two minutes; the word count does not. That 39 bits per second convergence means languages trade syllable rate against how much each syllable carries, so a Marathi or Hindi delivery of the same content is a different number of words.

Do not translate the 220-word English script word for word and assume it still times. Draft in the language you will speak, then time it aloud and cut.

To check the wording against the ritual, the [written Ganesh Chaturthi build guide](https://subhsandesh.in/guides/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) sets out the five offerings and the aarti order step by step.

## How to rehearse it so it holds under nerves

### 1. Read it aloud, never in your head

Reading aloud is measurably better for memory, and measured in this exact age group: in 7- to 10-year-olds, [recognition of words read aloud beat words read silently](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1111/cdev.13247) across two experiments, n = 41 and n = 40, for real words and invented ones alike. Silent revision is the wrong tool.

### 2. Time it three times with a phone

Record the first run and check the clock, not your instinct. First runs come in fast: nerves push the rate up, away from the 100 to 120 wpm you budgeted for.

### 3. Learn the four signposts, not the sentences

Memorise "three things — who, ten days, last day" and the closing line. If the middle wording slips, the map holds and you rebuild the sentence live. Word-for-word memorising makes a stumble unrecoverable.

### 4. Over-rehearse the first line and the last

Those are the two moments the room is fully listening, and the two you will be most nervous in. Get them past boredom; let the middle stay loose.

## Where a speech is the wrong choice, and where our page is too

If the slot is five minutes of class activity rather than a podium, a short reading with the class joining the aarti does more. And if a child genuinely cannot stand up in front of the hall, a written piece handed to the teacher beats a bad two minutes.

Our page is no substitute for the speech either: you send it afterwards, and it needs a phone and a link at the other end.

| What you hand the room | Time it takes | Platform-wide SubhSandesh data |
|---|---|---|
| A two-minute speech | 2 minutes, live | None — no Ganesh page data exists |
| A printed script | Their own reading pace | Not applicable |
| A Ganesh page sent after | ~90 seconds to perform | 49.6% of shared pages are opened on a phone (22,817 of 46,005 views) |

The first row is what matters: we have no Ganesh number to give you, and would rather say so than borrow one. Platform-wide, 96.0% of started pages are actually published and shared (3,737 of 3,894).

On leaving it late, the closest thing we have is a different festival. Of the 79 Raksha Bandhan 2026 pages finished in time, 55.7% were built on the day itself and 86.1% within 24 hours of it — but that is **Raksha Bandhan, not Ganesh Chaturthi**, a one-day festival against Ganesh Chaturthi's ten, and **n = 89 is small**, so no per-template, per-region or per-language rate can be drawn from it. Read it as a direction only: people prepare on the day, and a speech does not survive being written that morning.

To send something after the assembly: the [Ganesh Chaturthi page the recipient performs themselves](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) takes about as long to build as one rehearsal; [browse the rest](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) if this is not the occasion.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

## Sources

- Brysbaert, ["How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate"](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0749596X19300786), *Journal of Memory and Language* — 9 August 2019
- Li, ["Coping Strategies for Fast Delivery in Simultaneous Interpretation"](https://www.jostrans.org/article/view/7402), *The Journal of Specialised Translation* — 25 January 2010
- Pritchard, Heron-Delaney, Malone and MacLeod, ["The Production Effect Improves Memory in 7- to 10-Year-Old Children"](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdfdirect/10.1111/cdev.13247), *Child Development* — 17 May 2019
- Coupé, Oh, Dediu and Pellegrino, ["Different languages, similar encoding efficiency"](https://advances.sciencemag.org/content/advances/5/9/eaaw2594.full.pdf), *Science Advances* — 4 September 2019
